title: Elon Musk's Flying Roadster: How the Rocket Car Really Works

value.name: Tesla Roadster electric drivetrain
simplified: This blueprint uses the documented first-generation Tesla Roadster drivetrain architecture: a 53 kWh battery pack, power electronics, one three-phase induction motor, a single-speed gearbox and rear drive hardware.
The exact production dimensions of the newer Rocket Roadster drivetrain have not been published, so its thrusters, suction fans and any newer motor layout are omitted.
The battery-pack and component dimensions are simplified estimates for visual explanation; the overall first-generation Roadster dimensions are based on Tesla service data.
High-voltage cables, cooling pipes, software and internal battery cells are grouped into larger visible components.

value.name: Tesla Roadster fan-and-thruster system
simplified: The body size is an estimate of a low sports car because Tesla has not published a complete final dimension sheet for this configuration.
The internal battery, motors, fans, tanks and thruster positions are shown as an explanatory layout, not a confirmed production drawing.
The suction system holds the car against a surface by lowering pressure beneath it; it is not a lift fan.
The Rocket version is described by Tesla as a one-seat configuration with cold-gas thrusters around the car and is not approved for public-road use.
Only the general thruster arrangement is shown. No manufacturing details, pressures, nozzle dimensions or control software are included.
The flying demonstration proves a short controlled jump, not repeated practical flight or a certified flying car.

value.name: Rocket Roadster
simplified: The current Rocket Roadster does not have a published full dimension drawing, so the 4.8 m length, 2.0 m width and 1.2 m height are proportional estimates based on Tesla's sports-car form and older Roadster dimensions.
The model shows the Rocket configuration in a simplified cutaway: one seat, suction fans, ground sealing, compressed-gas tanks and perimeter cold-gas thrusters.
Tesla describes the Rocket version as invite-only and not approved for public road use.
The exact number, shape and internal mounting of fans, tanks, motors and thruster hardware are not fully published; grouped parts represent those systems without manufacturing detail.
The thrusters are shown as general directional nozzles only. Their pressure plumbing, valve design and detailed construction are omitted.

value.name: Rocket Roadster high-pressure tank
simplified: The exact Rocket Roadster tank drawings, pressure rating, vessel wall construction, pipe routing, and nozzle dimensions are not publicly published.

The reported Rocket layout uses a 400 L tank replacing the passenger seat and a 200 L tank elsewhere in the car; these volumes are represented here as approximate explanatory geometry, not manufacturing dimensions.
The tank is shown as a black composite pressure vessel because the available material list has no dedicated carbon-fiber-composite option.
The vehicle body dimensions and the positions of the tank, valves, pipes, and thrusters are estimated from the published descriptions and public images.
Only the general propulsion layout is shown: stored high-pressure gas flows through a manifold to cold-gas nozzles, and the exhaust direction produces the opposite vehicle motion.
This is an explainer model, not a buildable pressure system or a safety-certified vehicle design.

value.name: Tesla Roadster Rocket cold-gas nozzle cutaway
simplified: The Rocket Roadster’s final production dimensions and exact nozzle layout are not publicly specified, so the car proportions are estimated from the shown prototype and typical electric sports-car proportions.
The model shows representative cold-gas nozzles rather than all ten perimeter thrusters described for the Rocket version.
The pressure vessel is shown as one large composite-wrapped sphere; public reports differ on the exact number and arrangement of tanks.
Internal valves, regulators, control electronics, suspension, and detailed plumbing are omitted.
The nozzles are shown only as general tapered outlets to explain thrust direction, not as manufacturing drawings.
The suction fans and sealing skirt are included to distinguish ground-holding suction from rocket-like thrust.
